narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 92% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in your third year of law school had the greatest influence, followed by your LSAT score, then your first-year performance. All three pushed the model strongly toward predicting failure.

Your third-year grades placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked near the middle. This low ranking signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that is strongly associated with failing the bar. Similarly, your LSAT score of 26 is well below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, giving the model another clear reason to expect difficulty passing the bar. Your first-year grades, also in the bottom decile compared to an average around 6 for accepted students, added further weight in the same direction.

Taken together, these academic signals created a consistent picture that the model interpreted as a very high risk of bar exam failure.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas within your control. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, seeking targeted academic support or tutoring to improve your class ranking, and then reapplying once you have demonstrated clearer progress. Many students improve these metrics and gain admission on a later attempt.
